title: Operator Overloading and Special Members
objectives: Overload arithmetic, comparison and stream operators for a money type, choosing member vs free-function placement deliberately
Implement compound assignments returning references and define plain operators in terms of them
Describe the special member functions the compiler generates and control them with =default and =delete
Name the operators that cannot be overloaded and explain why operator<< must be a free function
motivation: A PnL engine that adds prices, scales notionals and compares bids lives or dies by operator discipline: mix a dollar value with a cents value and the blotter is quietly wrong. C++ lets your own types use the same operators as built-ins, so buy + sell or bid < ask means exactly what the class says it means. Along the way this lesson introduces the special member functions the compiler silently writes for every class, the machinery behind copies, assignments and destruction.

blocks.text: Operators are functions with punctuation names

blocks.md: Every overloadable operator is just a function: `a + b` resolves to either `a.operator+(b)` (member form) or `operator+(a, b)` (free form). Overloading exists so domain types read naturally: a Money type holding cents in a long long can support `+`, `-`, `==`, `<` and stream output, keeping every calculation inside the type instead of scattering conversion factors through the code. You cannot invent new operators, and you cannot change precedence, associativity or arity, you can only give an existing operator a meaning for your class.

blocks.caption: Run it: 14.25, then 11.25 after the commission, then 1 for buy < sell.

blocks.md: Design notes visible in the snippet. `operator+=` is a member returning `Money&` - returning `*this` lets assignments chain the way built-ins do. The free `operator+` is written **in terms of** `+=`, so the two operators can never drift apart semantically. Free (non-member) operators treat both sides symmetrically: if Money ever gained a non-explicit constructor from long long, `money + 5` and `5 + money` would both work through the free function, while a member `operator+` would only accept the left-hand form. `operator<<` has no choice at all: its left operand is a `std::ostream`, so it cannot be a member of Money, it must be a free function, returning the stream by reference so output chains.

blocks.title: Money in integer cents
blocks.md: Storing 4217.00 as long long cents 421700 avoids binary floating point entirely: adding and comparing cents is exact, so no 0.01 drift ever appears in an accumulation loop. Convert to decimal only at the boundary, exactly what the stream operator does.

blocks.text: The special members the compiler writes for you

blocks.md: Every class can have six **special member functions** generated on demand: default constructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment (covered in the move-semantics module) and destructor. The generated copy operations copy every member memberwise; the destructor runs its body, then destroys members in reverse declaration order. You only notice them when members are plain values, which is exactly when they are right, or when members are raw resources, where memberwise copying is a bug; the Rule of Three/Five lesson makes that systematic.

blocks.caption: Copy construction happens on initialization; assignment on an existing object (note: c ends up holding id 1). Destruction runs in reverse creation order: dtor 1, dtor 1, dtor 1.

blocks.md: Two keywords control generation. `= default` asks for the compiler-generated version explicitly, useful to keep a defaulted copy alongside a hand-written constructor. `= delete` forbids it: deleting the copy constructor and copy assignment makes a class non-copyable, the right answer for a process-wide RiskLimits object that must never be duplicated.

blocks.caption: Deleting copies turns a would-be runtime bug into a compile error.

blocks.text: What you cannot overload, and friendship

items: Cannot be overloaded: `.` (member access), `.*` (pointer-to-member access), `::` (scope resolution), `?:` (ternary), `sizeof` and `typeid` - they must mean what they mean for the type system to work.

Can be overloaded: arithmetic `+ - * / %`, comparisons `== != < > <= >=`, the compound family `+= -= *= ...`, subscript `[]`, function call `()`, increment/decrement, stream insertion/extraction and more.
Precedence, associativity and arity are fixed: `<<` stays left-associative, which is exactly why chained stream output works.

A free operator that must touch private members is declared a `friend` inside the class. Friendship is granted by the class, never taken, and it is neither inherited nor transitive. Prefer going through public accessors, the Money operator<< above needs no friend because it uses cents().

blocks.caption: Friendship is an alternative to accessors, use it sparingly.

guidedExercise.prompt: Extend the Money class with a unary `operator-()` member returning the negated amount, and a binary `Money operator*(long long n) const` scaling by an integer quantity of shares. In `main`: a position loses 8 cents per share, so start from `Money perLot{-8}`; compute `total = perLot * 250`, print it, then print `-total`. Expected output: `-20.00` then `20.00`.
hints: Unary minus is a member with no parameters: Money operator-() const.
Reuse the stream operator from the lesson; it already handles the sign and two-digit pennies.

independentExercise.prompt: A blotter sorts orders by notional. Write class `Order` with private `int qty_` and `double limitPx_`, a constructor, and `double notional() const`. Define `bool operator<(const Order&, const Order&)` as a free function comparing notionals. Put three orders in a `std::vector<Order>` - {3 lots at 101.5}, {10 at 42.0}, {2 at 250.0} - `std::sort` them, and print the smallest notional. Then answer in a comment: what would change if operator< were a member instead?
hints: The notionals are 3 x 101.5, 10 x 42.0 and 2 x 250.0; sort ascending, then print book.front().notional().
std::sort only needs operator< for Order; a member operator< would also work here because the left side of every comparison is an Order.

commonMistakes: Overloading operator+ but not operator+= (or vice versa) so the two drift apart; write += first and define + from it.
Returning by value from operator+= instead of returning *this as a reference, breaking chains and spawning copies.
Trying to overload ., ::, sizeof or ?:, they are not overloadable.
Making operator<< a member of your class; the left operand is the stream, so it must be a free function.
Forgetting the trailing return os; in a stream operator, which breaks chained output.
Leaving a one-argument constructor non-explicit and letting values convert silently between unit-bearing types.
realWorldApplication: Pricing libraries define arithmetic on Money, Yield, Spread and Volatility types so a bond math function cannot be handed a volatility where a spread belongs; the operators are overloaded once and the whole desk inherits the safety.
quantFinanceApplication: Integer-cent money arithmetic shown here is the same trick production trading systems use to keep cash accounting exact: store the smallest quoted unit, expose operators, convert to decimal only when printing or reporting.
summary: Operators are functions: compound/mutating operators work well as members; symmetric binary operators and operator<< belong to free functions.
Implement operator+= first and define operator+ in terms of it so the semantics exist in exactly one place.
The compiler generates default constructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, moves and destructor memberwise on demand; =default requests them, =delete forbids them.
operator<< must be a free function taking (std::ostream&, const T&) and returning the stream by reference.

quiz.prompt: Why must operator<< for Money be a free function rather than a member of Money?
options: Because operator<< cannot be overloaded at all
Because its left operand is a std::ostream, not a Money
Because member functions cannot return references
quiz.explanation: In the expression `cout << m` the left operand is the stream. A member operator<< would have to live in std::ostream, which you cannot modify, so the free function form `operator<<(std::ostream&, const Money&)` is the only option.

quiz.answer:
ctor 1
copy 1
ctor 2
assign 1
dtor 1
dtor 1
dtor 1
quiz.explanation: Ticket b = a is initialization of a new object (copy ctor); c = a is assignment on an existing object, which overwrites c.id_ with 1. Destruction runs in reverse creation order: c first, but its id is now 1 after the assignment, then b (1), then a (1). The "dtor 2" many people expect never appears because assignment changed the state before destruction.
First the free operator+ evaluates b + b, producing Tick{4}. Then the member operator+= adds it into a: 40 + 4 = 44, and the stream operator prints the value.

quiz.prompt: Which of these C++ operators cannot be overloaded for a user-defined class?
quiz.explanation: Member access (.), scope resolution (::), .*, ?:, sizeof and typeid are not overloadable. Function call operator() and operator< are ordinary, heavily used overloads.

quiz.prompt: A Money holds cents: buy at 421700, sell at 423125, then a commission of Money{-300} is added. What dollar amount does the final Money print as, in the format 12.34?
quiz.explanation: Cents: $423125 - 421700 = 1425$, then $1425 - 300 = 1125$ cents. The stream operator renders 1125 cents as 11.25.

quiz.prompt: Why implement operator+ as `Money r{a}; r += b; return r;` instead of duplicating the addition logic inside operator+?
quiz.modelAnswer: So the addition semantics live in exactly one place: operator+= holds the real logic and operator+ reuses it, guaranteeing the two operators stay consistent.
quiz.explanation: Defining + in terms of += gives both operators the same semantics by construction, removes duplicated code to test, and means a future fix to the addition logic automatically applies everywhere.

flashcards.front: Member vs free-function placement for overloaded operators
flashcards.back: Mutating/compound operators (+=, ++, [], ()) work naturally as members; symmetric binary operators and operator<< (stream is the left operand) belong to free functions.

flashcards.front: Money{-1525} printed through the lesson stream operator shows what?
flashcards.back: -15.25, the operator emits the sign, the whole dollars and two-digit pennies from a long long of cents.

flashcards.front: bool operator<(const Money& a, const Money& b) { return a < b; }: what is wrong?
flashcards.back: Infinite recursion: the body calls itself. It must compare the underlying data, e.g. a.cents() < b.cents().

flashcards.front: Which special member functions does the compiler generate on demand?
flashcards.back: Default constructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment and destructor, all memberwise, each generated only when used.

flashcards.front: = default vs = delete on a special member
flashcards.back: = default asks for the compiler-generated implementation explicitly; = delete forbids it, e.g. deleting the copy ctor/assignment to make a class non-copyable.
